results.title: SimpleSpread: Native, open source Mac spreadsheet | Product Hunt
results.content:
Hi Everyone,  
  
I wanted a spreadsheet on my Mac that opens fast, edits an .xlsx file and saves it back, and does nothing else. Numbers converts everything into its own format. Excel is a subscription and a big install for opening a CSV. Google Sheets wants a browser and an account.  
  
So I built SimpleSpread. It is a native Mac app, written entirely in Swift, and the whole spreadsheet stack is from scratch: the model, the formula engine, the XLSX reader and writer (down to the ZIP layer), CSV and the grid. The only outside library is Sparkle, for updates.  
  
• XLSX is the native format. Open a file from Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets, edit it, save it, send it back. Styles, number formats, formulas with cached values, merged ranges and frozen panes all survive the round trip. [...] • Notarized, and it updates itself in place.  
  
Upfront about what it is not: no charts, no pivot tables, no conditional formatting, no array formulas, no INDIRECT/OFFSET yet, and no collaboration. Frozen panes and merged cells are kept in the file but not drawn yet. It is Apple Silicon only, macOS 14 or later, and en-US number and date input for now.  
  
It's free, MIT licensed and on GitHub, so read it, fork it, send patches. I'd love to hear which missing feature stops you using it day to day. Find & Replace and Paste Values are next on my list. [...] SimpleSpread

results.content:

Review Simple Commenter?

Reviewers consistently say Simple Commenter succeeds by staying simple: it installs fast, is easy for non-technical clients to use, and cuts down messy feedback spread across email, Slack, screenshots, and calls. Agencies, designers, developers, and even PR users say it speeds revisions, keeps comments organized, and improves client engagement, sometimes helping stalled projects move again. A few specific touches stand out, like direct on-page comments, client links without sign-up, user restrictions, webhooks, and PDF support. The only notable criticism is occasional comment-placement glitches.
